521.event_title: Napoleon's mother and sister join him in exile on Elba
521.event: After his first abdication in 1814, Napoleon was sent to the small island of Elba and landed at its capital, Portoferraio, on 4 May 1814. His mother, Letizia Bonaparte, and his sister Pauline came to join him there, his mother living in a house in Portoferraio, while his wife Marie-Louise and their young son, for whom rooms had been prepared, never came. In 1818 his mother wrote to the Allied powers asking for his release from his final exile on Saint Helena, but her letter went unanswered.
521.explanation: When the emperor had lost his throne and the court that once surrounded him, it was his mother and sister who crossed the sea to share his exile, and his mother kept pleading for him long after his final defeat.
521.tie_back: The kural says that even when a man has lost everything he owned, his kin alone keep honouring the old bond, and Letizia Bonaparte did exactly that for her fallen son.
521._accuracy_note: A close fit: a ruler stripped of almost everything is still sought out and stood by chiefly by his own family.

522.event_title: Mayer Amschel Rothschild's five sons build a banking house across Europe
522.place: Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples
522.event: Mayer Amschel Rothschild, a Frankfurt dealer and banker, had five sons, all of whom entered the family business. The eldest, Amschel, stayed in Frankfurt, while Nathan established himself in England and founded N M Rothschild in London in 1809, James set up in Paris, Salomon in Vienna and Carl in Naples, and the brothers kept in close touch and worked together on major government loans. In 1810 the father made the Frankfurt firm a partnership with his sons, and in 1822 the Austrian emperor ennobled all five brothers.
522.explanation: Historians describe the five linked houses as working in effect like a single multinational bank, a strength that no one brother could have built on his own.
522.tie_back: The kural says kin whose affection never fails bring prosperity that keeps putting out new shoots, and the Rothschild brothers' cooperation across five cities made their family business grow far beyond its Frankfurt beginnings.
522._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of wealth multiplying through loyal, cooperating kin, which is the kural's exact point.

523.event_title: The Inca civil war between Huascar and Atahualpa
523.event: After the Inca ruler Huayna Capac died in an epidemic without a clearly settled successor, his sons Huascar, based at Cuzco, and Atahualpa, based in the north at Quito, fought a long civil war for the throne. The war divided the Inca nobility and armies and was costly to both sides, and Atahualpa's generals finally captured Huascar in 1532. Only months later, in November 1532, a small Spanish force under Francisco Pizarro captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca, and the empire soon fell under Spanish rule.
523.explanation: Historians count the brothers' war, together with epidemic disease and Spanish weapons, among the reasons the largest empire in the Americas collapsed so quickly.
523.tie_back: The kural compares a man who does not live heart to heart with his kin to a wide tank without banks, and the quarrel between royal brothers left the Inca realm unable to hold on to what it had built.
523._accuracy_note: A clear case of kin discord draining a realm, though the Spanish conquest had several causes and the kural speaks of an individual's household wealth.

524.event_title: Christian IX and Queen Louise gather their family at Fredensborg each summer
524.event: King Christian IX of Denmark and Queen Louise saw their children marry into many of Europe's royal houses: their daughters included Alexandra, later Queen of the United Kingdom, and Dagmar, Empress of Russia, and their son George became King George I of Greece. Every summer the couple, known as Europe's parents-in-law, gathered their children, their children's spouses and their many grandchildren at Fredensborg Palace. The painter Laurits Tuxen recorded these Fredensborg Days in a group portrait about five by seven metres, made in 1883-1886, which now hangs in Christiansborg Palace in Copenhagen.
524.explanation: The king of a small country found the true reward of his position in a family circle that stretched across the continent and returned to him year after year.
524.tie_back: The kural says the real fruit of gaining wealth and standing is to live surrounded by one's kin, and Christian IX's summers at Fredensborg were exactly such a life.
524._accuracy_note: A vivid picture of a ruler literally encircled by kin; the kural's link between wealth and kin is implied rather than shown.

525.event_title: Moshoeshoe gathers scattered peoples into the Basotho nation
525.event: During the wars and migrations that convulsed Southern Africa in the early nineteenth century, the chief Moshoeshoe led his people to the nearly impregnable mountain stronghold of Thaba Bosiu. His following grew as other African peoples were drawn by the protection he could provide, and he had a reputation for generous treatment of allies and enemies alike. He united these groups of refugees into the Sotho (Basotho) nation, and he is regarded today as the father of Lesotho.
525.explanation: Moshoeshoe built a nation not from a single bloodline but by drawing ever more peoples into his circle through protection and generous dealing.
525.tie_back: The kural says one who can both give freely and deal kindly will be surrounded by kin, circle upon circle, and Moshoeshoe's generosity turned scattered refugees into one people.
525._accuracy_note: Strong on generosity widening the circle of followers; the kind-speech half of the kural is reflected in his diplomacy but not separately documented here.

526.event_title: Cyrus the Great lets deported peoples return home
526.event: After the Persian king Cyrus the Great captured Babylon in 539 BCE, a proclamation inscribed in his name on a clay cylinder recorded how he restored shrines and allowed deported peoples to return to their homes, reversing the policy of earlier Assyrian and Babylonian kings. It is thought to have been at this time that the Judaeans returned to Jerusalem to rebuild their Temple. About a century later the Greek historian Herodotus recorded that the Persians called Cyrus a father, because he was gentle and devised good things for them, while they called his son Cambyses a master.
526.explanation: Instead of keeping the peoples his predecessors had uprooted in captivity, Cyrus gave them back their homes and gods, and his own people remembered him as a father rather than a master.
526.tie_back: The kural says no one on earth has more people at his side than one who gives freely and does not nurse anger, and Cyrus won lasting loyalty through generosity rather than vengeance.
526._accuracy_note: The policy and the reputation are both well documented, though the cylinder is royal propaganda and the kural's 'kin' is read here broadly as the people at a ruler's side.

527.event_title: Fan Zhongyan founds the Fan clan charitable estate
527.event: Fan Zhongyan, a Song-dynasty scholar-official from Suzhou who had been orphaned of his father in infancy, used his own funds late in his career to buy farmland near his home town and set it up as a charitable estate for his clan. Rents from the land supplied grain to members of the Fan lineage and helped them meet the costs of weddings, funerals and schooling. The estate continued for centuries and became a model for later lineage trusts in China.
527.explanation: Rather than keep the fruits of his success for his own household, Fan arranged for the whole clan to share in them, and his example shaped Chinese kinship institutions for generations.
527.tie_back: The kural praises the crow that does not hide its food but calls its kin to share it, and Fan Zhongyan's estate turned his own prosperity into a meal for the whole clan.
527._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the crow image: wealth deliberately shared with the whole kin group, with lasting prosperity for the clan.

528.event_title: Peter the Great issues the Table of Ranks
528.event: Peter the Great's Table of Ranks arranged Russia's military, naval and civil services into a hierarchy of fourteen grades and based promotion on personal ability and performance rather than on birth and family descent. Anyone who reached the eighth rank gained the status of a hereditary noble, which caused resentment among parts of the old aristocracy that lost its exclusive claim to high office. With minor changes, the system remained in use until 1917.
528.explanation: By ranking servants of the state according to service and merit, Peter tied capable people of many backgrounds to the throne while keeping a clear order of precedence.
528.tie_back: The kural says a king who gives each person the regard their merit deserves, rather than treating everyone the same, will have many staying by him, and the Table of Ranks wrote merit-based, graded regard into law.
528._accuracy_note: A good match for regard according to merit, though the kural concerns a ruler's kin and the Table governed state servants generally.

529.event_title: Hungary is reconciled with the Habsburg crown in the Compromise of 1867
529.event: After the Hungarian revolution of 1848-49 was put down, Hungary was ruled directly from Vienna, and many Hungarians answered with stubborn passive resistance, boycotting the imperial parliament set up in 1861. Led by the moderate Ferenc Deak, who insisted on Hungary's constitutional rights, Hungary negotiated the Compromise (Ausgleich) concluded on 8 February 1867, under which Emperor Franz Joseph gave Hungary full internal self-government with its own responsible ministry, while Hungary accepted that the empire remain a single state for war and foreign affairs. On 8 June 1867 Franz Joseph was crowned King of Hungary in Buda.
529.explanation: Once the grievance that had driven Hungary away, rule without its constitution, was removed, the estranged kingdom returned to its allegiance to the dynasty.
529.tie_back: The kural says those who left because of a grievance come back of their own accord once its cause is gone, and Hungary returned to its crowned king when its constitution was restored.
529._accuracy_note: A reasonable political parallel to estranged kin returning once the cause of the rift is removed, though a nation is not literally kin and the return was negotiated rather than spontaneous.

530.event: In 415 BCE the Athenian general Alcibiades, recalled from the expedition to Sicily to face charges of sacrilege, fled to Sparta, Athens's enemy, and advised the Spartans; he later went over to the Persian governor Tissaphernes. After leading the Athenian fleet to victories in the Hellespont, he returned to Athens in triumph in 407 BCE, the old charges were dropped, and he was given supreme command above all other generals. When a subordinate he had left in charge of the fleet lost a battle to the Spartans at Notium in 406 BCE, Alcibiades was not re-elected general and withdrew to Thrace.
530.explanation: Athens restored a former defector to the highest command almost at once, without lasting trust on either side, and the arrangement collapsed within about a year.
530.tie_back: The kural advises a ruler to meet the needs of a kinsman who left and came back for his own purposes, but to weigh him carefully before taking him back, and Athens's haste with Alcibiades shows what happens when that weighing is skipped.
530._accuracy_note: A useful cautionary illustration of a returning deserter taken back too readily, though Alcibiades did have a reason to flee (the charges) and was a fellow citizen rather than a kinsman.
